statement: A row in a cinema has 10 seats. Three friends want to sit in three seats next to each other in that row. How many different groups of three seats could they choose?

choices.misconception: I took away 1 from 10, as if they needed only two seats next to each other.
I counted one group starting at every seat, but a group cannot start at seat 9 or 10.
I found the 8 groups and then multiplied by 3 because there are 3 friends, but each group is just one choice of seats.
I counted the 8 groups and also the 6 orders the friends can sit in, but the question only asks which seats.

hints: Where can the leftmost seat of the group be?
Counting by position: name each group by its first seat, then find the last seat a group of three can start at without running off the row.
A group can start at seat 1, 2, 3 and so on, up to seat 8, which uses seats 8, 9 and 10.

solutions.reliable: Name each group by its leftmost seat. Starting at seat 1 uses seats 1, 2, 3. Starting at seat 8 uses seats 8, 9, 10. Starting at seat 9 would need a seat 11, which does not exist. So the starting seat is 1, 2, ..., 8, giving 8 groups. The transferable idea: a block of length $k$ in a row of $n$ fits in $n - k + 1$ positions.

whyOnTest: Sliding a block along a row and counting its starting places is the basic move behind every counting by position problem.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
